nameStory: The maple looper moth gets its name from its caterpillar's distinctive way of moving, which resembles the 'looping' or inchworm motion as it arches its back to bring its rear legs forward to meet its front legs. The 'maple' part comes from one of its favorite host trees, though these caterpillars aren't picky eaters and will happily munch on birch and walnut too.
description: The maple looper moth is a medium-sized brown moth that's often overlooked despite being fairly common throughout New England. With wings spanning about 1.3 to 1.7 inches across, it has a modest, earth-toned appearance that helps it blend into tree bark during the day. This moth belongs to a large family that includes some of our most dramatic moths, though the maple looper tends toward subtlety rather than flash. You're most likely to spot adults from spring through early fall, as they're active for much of the growing season.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive double stripe pattern across the forewings that gives this species its scientific name 'bistriaris' - the wings feel papery and delicate when examined closely

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Wingspan measures between 1.3-1.7 inches, making it noticeably larger than many common yard moths but smaller than the dramatic sphinx moths

idTips.label: Body coloration
idTips.description: The body appears muted brown to grayish-brown, with a soft, fuzzy texture typical of night-flying moths - feels almost velvety if gently touched

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings have a matte finish rather than glossy, with scales that can rub off easily onto your fingers if handled

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest during the day, holds wings in a tent-like position over the body, often pressed tightly against tree bark with remarkable camouflage

habitat: Look for maple looper moths in mixed deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially where maples, birches, and walnuts grow together. They're equally at home in suburban areas with mature shade trees and can often be found around porch lights or outdoor lighting near wooded areas. These moths prefer the forest edge and clearings rather than deep, dense woods.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April and can be spotted at lights or resting on tree bark during warm evenings. This is when you'll first see the fresh, newly-emerged moths with crisp wing patterns.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity continues through summer months, with adults commonly attracted to artificial lights on warm nights. Look for them resting on tree trunks during the day, perfectly camouflaged against bark.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into September, though numbers typically decline as temperatures drop. Late-season individuals may appear more worn, with faded colors and tattered wing edges.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; the species overwinters in another life stage. No moths will be visible during the cold months.

funFact: Despite being called the 'maple' looper moth, the caterpillars are actually quite the gourmets - they'll feast on at least three different tree families (maple, birch, and walnut), making them one of nature's less picky eaters in a world where many moth caterpillars specialize on just one plant species!
confusionNotes: Maple looper moths can be confused with other medium-sized brown moths in the same family, but the double-stripe pattern on the forewings is your best clue. Remember: 'bi-striaris' means 'two stripes' - if you can make out two parallel lines crossing the wing, you're likely looking at a maple looper.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'bistriaris' literally means 'two-striped,' directly referencing the moth's most distinctive field mark. This is one of those helpful cases where the Latin name actually gives you a clear identification hint rather than honoring some long-dead naturalist!
compareHints: Since the maple looper moth is the only member of its genus Parallelia in our region, compare it with other medium-sized brown moths in the Erebidae family. Unlike the dramatic underwing moths that flash bright colors when startled, maple loopers keep their subdued coloration on both wing surfaces. They're also smaller and less robust than many of their flashier cousins in this diverse moth family.
